doc.title: Michael Moore interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Working with Gene Bertoncini and the value of arranged groups
summary: Moore explains why he likes Bertoncini's arrangements and laments the lack of rehearsed bands, citing Nat Cole, Goodman and the Barnes-Braff quartet.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: What is it about his playing that’s kept you two together for so many years?

Well I think number one he gets jobs, but I think the thing is that he has a great sense of arranging for the two instruments, again, featuring the bass in a very nice way. And he encouraged me to do things with the bow that I hadn’t done, and he came up with — really, most of the time I don’t like jazz and classical mixed together. I find that usually it doesn’t work for one reason or the other. It takes away from both. But his arrangements seem to work as far as the integrity of both. The classical part was done with integrity, and the jazz was separate enough that that worked. And the timbre of the two instruments, the classical guitar with the bass, it was unusual. I think one of the things that I miss nowadays in music, that there are very few bands around anymore. There are very few arranged groups. And that is for a lot of reasons, economic reasons mostly. And I think that’s one of the things that really encouraged me to keep working with Gene is we had material worked out. We have a good repertoire, and we knew — it’s nice to go out on the bandstand, for me, and know what you’re going to do, and to have the confidence that you’re going to get out there and you’re going to have material that’s going to make it a nice performance for the people, whether you’re having a good night as far as improvisation is concerned, or not. You know you’re going to be able to go over.

I really enjoy hearing a combo or small ensemble that is basically a jazz unit but every once in a while they’ll do something that you know has been arranged and rehearsed. I think it really adds a lot of the performance that that group took the time to do that.
I feel the same way. Like T.S. Monk’s band, you know Thelonious Monk Junior, I mean I heard them and they have arrangements and they’re not reading music, they have their

act together. And the improvisation is very good, but there are a lot of great improvisers around nowadays, but there are very few bands. And my looking back in history, I mean I grew up with the Nat Cole Trio. My father had a trio based like that, on that kind of thing, and those tight arrangements. And Benny Goodman’s trios and quartets and all the groups that I admired as I grew up were very well thought out and very well rehearsed, and the improvisation was a great part of it but so were the arrangements. That was why like one of the bands that I worked with in my young years which was so important to me which was George Barnes and Ruby Braff, the quartet record. We rehearsed a lot, and the music shows it, and I still listen to those things and they still sound fresh and good to me because of that.
